intro: You're looking for an accountant who understands limited liability partnerships, and you want one nearby. An LLP is its own kind of business, with filing duties at Companies House and a partnership return for HMRC, so it helps to speak to someone who deals with LLPs regularly. We can introduce you to a UK accountant suited to your LLP, and they will quote you directly.

context_heading: One key thing to understand about LLP accountants
context: The word accountant is not a protected title in the UK, so anyone can call themselves one. Protected titles include Chartered Accountant (ICAEW, ICAS or Chartered Accountants Ireland), Chartered Certified Accountant (ACCA) and Chartered Management Accountant (CIMA), and members of those bodies are bound by their ethics, training and complaints rules. Only a registered auditor can sign a statutory audit report.

Every accountancy practice must also be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes, either by a professional body or by HMRC. It is reasonable to ask which body supervises a firm, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance, and how complaints are handled.

faqs.q: Do I need a special accountant for an LLP?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but an accountant who deals with LLPs regularly will be familiar with the partnership return, members' Self Assessment and the salaried member rules. It is worth asking how often they work with LLPs.

faqs.q: What is the salaried member rules test?
faqs.a: The salaried member rules can affect whether a member of an LLP is taxed as employed or self-employed. The tests look at the member's role and remuneration, and an accountant can explain how they apply to your members.

LLP SORP is the Statement of Recommended Practice for limited liability partnerships, which sets out how their accounts should be prepared. If your LLP prepares accounts under it, your accountant should be able to explain what it involves.

extra_heading: Choosing between LLP accountants close to you
extra: Searching for an LLP accountant near me suggests you want someone you can meet face to face rather than deal with entirely at a distance, which matters when LLP accounts and members' tax positions need explaining properly. Nearby is a practical starting point, but it is not the same as suitable, so weigh location alongside whether the practice actually deals with limited liability partnerships.

When you compare, ask each accountant to talk you through how they would approach your LLP's accounts, the partnership return and the members' Self Assessment returns, and whether the salaried member rules are something they handle routinely. Ask too about LLP SORP if it applies to you, and about which body supervises the firm for anti-money-laundering purposes and whether they hold professional indemnity insurance. A practice that answers these clearly and in plain language is easier to judge than one that simply advertises being close by.

At a first meeting, expect to bring your LLP agreement, any previous accounts and returns, and details of what each member takes out of the partnership. The accountant will usually want to understand the members' roles and pay before advising on tax status, so having that to hand makes the conversation more useful. Their quote will be price on application, and you are free to speak to more than one before deciding.

extra_faqs.q: Does it matter if my LLP accountant is nearby?
extra_faqs.a: Not always, but local can help if you prefer meeting in person or dropping off records. What matters more is whether the practice regularly deals with LLP accounts, the partnership return and members' tax positions.

extra_faqs.q: Should I choose an accountant who is closest to me?
extra_faqs.a: Distance is only one factor. Compare how clearly each explains LLP filing at Companies House, the partnership return for HMRC and the salaried member rules, and check which body supervises them and whether they hold professional indemnity insurance.
